newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Albright sets U.S. conditions for NATO membership.
newsitem.headline: Albright sets U.S. conditions for NATO membership.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright set out U.S. priorities for new NATO members on Thursday and insisted that countries not chosen for membership this year must be given assurances that the alliance door remains open.

In remarks prepared for a NATO foreign ministers meeting that is laying important ground for alliance expansion, she said new members must meet the highest possible standards before they join and be able to contribute to NATO's common security.

Although Albright did not say so explicitly in the written statement, her remarks were meant to underscore the U.S. view that only Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic should be invited to join NATO when the alliance's 16 leaders meet in Madrid on July 8-9.
Romania and Slovenia have also pushed hard for admission but Washington wants to keep them for a second round.
"First we want to make NATO stronger and more cohesive by adding new allies who are eager and able to contribute to our common security," Albright said.

"We want the first round of enlargement to be seen as a solid success in these terms and we want to be backed by strong parliamentary and public majorities," she said in her statement, made available by the State Department.

NATO "must continue to insist that the candidates for membership in NATO meet the highest possible standards before they are invited to join. The alliance should admit only those new democracies that have both cleared the highest hurdles of reform and demonstrated they can meet the full obligations of membership.
"NATO enlargement is not a scholarship programme," Albright said.
France is supporting Romania's bid for admission and the Americans acknowledge that Bucharest has made important strides since a democratic election last year.

But Washington, concerned that Romania's turn toward democracy be given more time to prove its staying power, wants to see more economic and political reforms. There is also concern that Romania would have difficulty in paying its share of NATO expansion costs.
Slovenia, backed by Italy and other countries, would be better able to its way as an alliance member but its army is small.

With these and other NATO aspirants in mind, Albright stressed that "we must make a clear and credible commitment in Madrid to those nations that are not yet ready for membership...They need to be certain that there is no invisible barrier across the open door we have pledged."

To this end, she argued that "it is essential that NATO begins a new phase of dialogues with aspiring countries after Madrid (because this would be) the most clear signal of NATO's intentions on enlargement in the years ahead."
Some have suggested that, after Madrid, NATO should take a pause -- even as long as a few years -- before considering another round of new members.

Albright said: "We cannot promise any country that it will one day join NATO. But we can offer a process that gives substance to the commitments we have made, one that helps aspiring nations understand what they must do and how they must change to make membership a possibility."

Regardless of what NATO leaders decide in Madrid, the U.S. Senate and legislatures in other alliance capitals will have the final say on expansion and Albright stressed the need to "bring our legislators into this process."
She also said the alliance had to be serious and forthright about the costs of enlargement, estimated at billions of dollars.
